title: Storage Classes: auto, static, extern, register
html:
A storage-class specifier decides where a variable lives, how long it lives (lifetime) and who can see it (linkage).

SpecifierLifetimeDefault valueScope / linkageTypical use
auto (default for locals)Until the block endsGarbageBlock, no linkageOrdinary local variables
static (local)Whole program0Block, no linkageRemember a value between calls
static (global / function)Whole program0File only (internal linkage)Hide helpers from other files
externWhole program0 (where defined)All files (external linkage)Share a global across files
registerUntil the block endsGarbageBlockHistoric hint; cannot take its address
_Thread_local (C11)Per thread0As aboveOne copy per thread

static local: state that survives calls

static at file level: private to the file

extern: one definition, many declarations

Key point

Put extern int shared; in a header, and int shared = 0; in exactly one .c file. Functions are extern by default, so extern on a prototype is redundant.

register

Modern compilers ignore register for optimisation — they allocate registers far better than humans. Its only remaining effect is forbidding &. (auto in C means “automatic storage”; C23 repurposes it for type inference like C++.)

What are the differences between a static local variable and a global variable?

Both have static storage duration (they live for the whole program and are zero-initialised). A static local is only visible inside its function (block scope), whereas a global is visible to the whole file and — unless declared static — to other files via extern.

What does static mean for a function?

It gives the function internal linkage: it can only be called from the translation unit that defines it. This is C’s way of making a function private and avoids name clashes between files.

Can a static variable be initialised with a non-constant expression?

No, not in C. Objects with static storage duration must be initialised with constant expressions because the initial values are baked into the executable’s data segment before main runs. (C++ allows dynamic initialisation.)
